blocks.text: More than 20 million carbon compounds are known today, and most are studied in organic chemistry, which IUPAC describes as the study of compounds containing carbon in which carbon is bonded to itself, to hydrogen or to other elements, excluding some inorganic compounds. Carbonates, cyanides (e.g. KCN), carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide are traditionally treated as inorganic. Organic compounds usually have low melting and boiling points, low densities and low solubility in water.

blocks.title: Catenation
blocks.text: Catenation is the ability of atoms of the same element to link to one another (from the Latin catena, chain). Carbon forms long chains and rings through stable C-C covalent bonds.

Because carbon is tetravalent (forms four bonds), its atoms can be arranged in many different ways. Even four carbon atoms can be joined in four different arrangements. Catenation explains why organic compounds can be large and complex and why there are so many of them.

blocks.alt: Four arrangements of four carbon atoms, each C joined by single lines: a straight chain C-C-C-C; a chain of three C with a fourth C hanging below the middle one; four C at the corners of a square; and a triangle of three C with a fourth C above the top one.
